prompt:
You maintain a running summary of a long engineering document that is being read part by part, so that a later reader can model the system in SysML v2 without seeing the earlier parts.
Update the summary with the new part. Keep, as compactly as possible: the full names of system elements, actors and items; every alias or call sign with the full name it stands for; which element produces, sends or receives which item; modes and normative requirements. At most 300 words.

Current summary:
Context: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) NextGen program seeks increased National Airspace System (NAS) capacity and efficiency. Area navigation, direct routing, and air traffic automation upgrades support efficient en route operations in fair weather; adverse-weather operations remain constrained by automation limitations, policies, and procedures. Adverse weather includes convection/thunderstorms, winds, turbulence, snow/ice, and visibility/low ceilings; it causes roughly 70% of US operational delays.
Actors/elements: FAA; FAA traffic managers; FAA air traffic control system; controllers; aircraft; flight operators; general public; NASA; industry and other air traffic management (ATM) stakeholders. NASA surveyed stakeholders in 2015, identifying weather-related en route delays and interruptions as the most significant and costly issue.
Operational conditions: fair weather versus adverse weather, especially significant convective activity (not specified as formal system modes).
Items/interactions: During significant convection, FAA traffic managers use severe weather avoidance plans, also called Playbook routes, to divert aircraft traffic safely around weather-impacted regions. These strategic plans are devised at least two hours before departure, provide predictability, and introduce substantial deviations from nominal routes. Existing automation does not notify traffic managers when weather constraints change and avoidance routes may no longer be needed; aircraft consequently fly farther, increasing time, fuel use, costs, and environmental impacts.
Proposed system: NASA’s Airspace Technology Demonstrations 3 (ATD-3) project assembles an integrated suite of ground- and aircraft-based technologies and decision-making aids to continuously search for more efficient weather-avoidance routes and respond rapidly to weather changes and associated traffic management initiatives. Future traffic demand motivates a more efficient, integrated traffic management system and controller tools that leverage human productivity. No explicit normative requirements or detailed item interfaces are specified yet.

New part:
U0014: These route efficiency enhancements are targeted at en route airspace and will enable continued use of en route and arrival metering in the presence of weather.
U0015: NASA’s Dynamic Weather Routes (DWR) concept represents a subset of those technologies and focuses primarily on the cruise phase of flight.
U0016: It leverages existing air traffic weather, airspace, and traffic data, as well as improvements in navigation, surveillance, communication and digital network technologies, and builds upon existing ATM automation to address the shortcomings associated with strategic traffic flow management initiatives and weather forecasting uncertainties.
U0017: The potential benefits in the form of time, fuel, and cost savings are significant.
U0018: This concept of operations synopsis provides a detailed description of DWR, its potential benefits and notional implementation paths. 3 CURRENT SYSTEM - SHORTFALLS In today’s operations, Traffic Management Initiatives, or TMIs, are necessary to ensure aircraft safely avoid areas of adverse weather and to meter traffic when demand in a given area exceeds air traffic control’s capacity to safely separate aircraft.
U0019: Although necessary for safety, route diversions and metering can be overly conservative due to uncertainty in weather forecasts and air traffic control capacity limitations in sectors adjacent to the weather.
U0020: When significant convective activity is forecasted to develop in an area of the NAS, FAA traffic managers identify those areas as Flow Constrained Area (FCA), and may implement Severe Weather Avoidance Plans (SWAP), or Playbook routes, to safely divert traffic around those weather-impacted regions.
U0021: Playbook routes are identified 2 to 8 hours prior to the time the constraint is predicted to develop, to provide traffic managers and aircraft operators with ample time to prepare and assign the necessary resources where needed.
U0022: This lead time combined with uncertainties in weather forecasts often results in overly conservative deviations around actual weather.
U0023: Playbook routes tend to be very conservative both geographically and temporally to account for uncertainties in forecast accuracy.
U0024: This typically results in the selected playbook routes giving predicted weather-impacted areas a wide berth to account for those forecast uncertainties, and helps minimize subsequent changes, which can be complicated and time-consuming to implement once the SWAP routes are in play.

Return JSON {"summary": "..."}.
